Mutating a list while iterating over it skips elements: `for entry in entries` advances an index each loop, and `entries.remove(entry)` shifts subsequent items left, so the item right after any removed one gets skipped and stays in the output even if disabled.

Mutating a list while iterating it skips elements: `entries.remove(entry)` shifts subsequent items left, so the iterator advances past one unremoved disabled entry each time it removes something — some disabled entries survive.
Mutating a list while iterating skips elements: removing index i shifts index i+1 into i's slot, so the loop's next index skips it — a disabled entry right after a removed one survives.

Skips entries: removing from a list while iterating shifts indices, so the entry right after each disabled one gets skipped on the next iteration — e.g. `[{enabled:False}, {enabled:False}]` leaves the second one in the output.

Script does not terminate at that grep. `check` is the condition of `if check; then`, so `set -e` is suspended for every command inside it (per bash's documented exemption for commands whose status feeds an `if`/`while`/`until` test) — grep's failure is swallowed, `echo checked` still runs, and `check` returns `echo`'s exit status (0) regardless of grep's result, so `deploy` runs even when `ready` isn't in the status file.

Script doesn't terminate at grep — `set -e` is suspended for any command whose exit status feeds an `if` test, and that suspension propagates into the whole function body when the function itself is the tested command. Worse, `check`'s return status comes from `echo checked` (its last command), not from `grep`, so `if check` evaluates true and calls `deploy` even when grep fails to find "ready".

Script doesn't terminate at grep — `check` is the condition of an `if`, and `set -e` is suspended for commands in that position (per bash's documented exemption), so grep's non-zero exit doesn't trigger the errexit trap.

More important bug: `echo checked` still runs after grep fails (no `&&` between them), and its exit status (0) becomes `check`'s return value — so `if check` is always true and `deploy` runs even when grep finds nothing.
